correctness.rationale: The proof correctly starts from the published exhaustive A/B/C-plus-40 classification of near-perfect numbers with two prime factors. Because an even base makes the repunit factor odd, Type A forces that factor to be either the Mersenne prime or its square; the single-prime option violates the digit bound, while the square option and Ljunggren's repunit-square theorem exclude every length above two. Type B makes the digit too large. Type C forces the odd repunit factor to equal its odd prime; if length were at least three, \(U_n>g^2>a^2=2^{2t-2}\ge2^t>q\), contradiction. The isolated 40 is excluded directly. Substitution proves both converse families, and the package verifier correctly supplies only finite regression checks.

value.rationale: Repdigit near-perfect numbers are an established research object, and extending a finite-base theorem to every even base while obtaining an exhaustive parametric classification is a natural structural advance. The result explains exactly why two of the four general two-prime types cannot occur and why all surviving repdigits have two digits.
residual_risks: Odd bases and three-or-more-prime-factor repdigits remain open outside the claim.

final_claim: For every even base \(g\), any near-perfect repdigit \(N=a(1+g+\cdots+g^{n-1})\) with \(n\ge2\) and exactly two distinct prime factors has \(n=2\), and it belongs exactly to one of two explicit families: the Type-A Mersenne-square family \(g=(2^p-1)^2-1, a=2^{p-1}\), or the Type-C family \(g+1=2^t-2^k-1\) prime with \(a=2^{t-1}\) and the stated digit inequality.
limitations: The classification assumes exactly two distinct prime factors.
